g.passage: Good nature is something born with us--an easy, contented disposition, and a tendency to take things quietly and pleasantly. We inherit it. There is little merit in possessing it. Good humor is the result of pleasant surroundings and agreeable circumstances. A good-humored man is so when everything goes right; when things go wrong, his good humor departs and bad humor takes its place. But good temper results from training and self-control--keeping constant watch over our passions and feelings, and above all being in constant harmony with God; for he who is at peace with God is at peace with man, and will keep the "even tenor of his way."

g.explanation: 지문은 good nature, good humor, good temper를 차례로 구분하며 독자가 훈련과 자제를 통해 좋은 기질을 길러야 한다고 진지하게 가르친다. 'results from training and self-control'과 'in constant harmony with God' 같은 표현이 교훈적이고 진지한 태도를 보여 주므로 A가 정답이다. B는 누군가를 비난하는 표현이 없어 틀리다. C는 조롱이나 장난스러운 표현이 없고, D는 필자가 자신의 주장에 확신을 갖고 있어 틀리다.

g.passage: You will soon be as well as ever, and we shall all be rejoiced at your return. You must not, however, become impatient at the gradual progress you must necessarily make, but be content with the steady advance you are making to health and strength. Your progress will be the more certain and your recovery more confirmed. Do not let Sherman capture you, and I will endeavor to hold Grant till you come. I am glad to hear such good accounts of my little namesake. Good lungs are a great blessing, and nothing expands them better than a full, hearty yell. I hope Mrs. Longstreet is well, and that she is enjoying the good peaches and melons of Georgia.

g.passage: Though I have traveled close to a million miles behind the iron horse I cannot ride backwards on a railroad train. In that respect I am like the husband who when about to die said to his wife: "I want to make a special request of you, and that is, see that I am buried face down; it always did make me sick to travel backwards." When a boy I could not swing as could other boys. My head is not level on my shoulders. I have never crossed the ocean and never will. I cannot ride the rolling waves. Some years ago when out on a little coast ride for pleasure, (if that's what you call it) I said to the captain: "How long till we reach the shore?"

g.passage:
In France, mothers always visit with their daughters; and if restraint upon unmarried people is carried to excess there, we certainly err on the opposite extreme. We allow too much freedom, and we allow it too soon. I believe it is much better for a very young lady never to go about alone, or visit for any length of time from home, without her mother.

Youth must have friends, and those friends, being loved ardently, will have prodigious influence. The choice requires extreme caution. The whole of human destiny is often materially affected by those with whom we are intimate at fourteen or fifteen years of age.
g.question: Based on the text, how does the author view the ideal relationship between a very young lady and her mother?
options: The mother should serve as a close guide who accompanies her daughter.
The daughter should act as an equal who travels freely without her mother.
The mother should remain a distant authority who is consulted only rarely.
The daughter should let her friends replace her mother as her chief guide.
g.explanation: 필자는 프랑스에서는 어머니가 늘 딸과 함께 방문한다고 소개하고, 어린 숙녀는 'never to go about alone'해야 하며 어머니 없이 집을 떠나지 말아야 한다고 주장한다. 또한 열넷, 열다섯 살의 친구 선택이 운명을 좌우하므로 매우 신중해야 한다고 덧붙인다. 따라서 어머니가 곁에서 이끄는 동반자여야 한다는 A가 정답이다. B는 필자가 지나친 자유를 비판하므로 틀리고, C와 D는 어머니의 동행을 강조하는 주장과 반대된다.

g.passage:
There is a fascination in it; there is a magnetism stronger than that of the rock which drew the nails from Sindbad's ship. You are like a bird let out with a string tied to the foot to flutter a little way and return again. It is not business, for you may have none, in the ordinary sense; it is not "society," it is not pleasure. It is the presence of man in his myriads. There is something in the heart which cannot be satisfied away from it.

It is a curious thing that your next-door neighbour may be a stranger, but there are no strangers in a vast crowd.

the loneliness a person feels when living beside an unknown neighbor.

the burden of business duties that keep a person tied to an office.

g.passage:
The hot, sleepy streets were waking up in the red glow of the fading day. People in the town, now that the glare had died from their eyes, were telling each other that the air was cool, and trying to believe it.

Outside, however, the assertion had more truth in it. A ripple of refreshment was slowly spreading up from the distant river. The shadows of the straight-lined trees lay across the brick road in great black stripes. The fields looked as if their dusty grass was turning green again beneath the darkening sky; in the dull ditches stood the cattle, dreamily content.

The girls walked on in silence till they reached a point where the road swerved off into a little thicket. This was the spot which Romeo must have had in his mind.

options: a coming storm that threatens the girls on their walk to the thicket.
a false hope that the townspeople invent to forget the summer heat.
a sign that the fields have been ruined by a long season of drought.
a gentle relief that arrives as the oppressive day finally ends.
g.explanation: 지문 앞부분에서 마을 사람들은 공기가 시원하다고 'trying to believe it'하지만, 바깥에서는 그 말이 'had more truth in it'이라고 한다. 강에서 퍼지는 상쾌함과 함께 풀이 다시 푸르러 보이고 소들이 'dreamily content'한 모습은 무더운 하루 끝에 찾아온 안도를 나타낸다. 따라서 D가 정답이다. A는 폭풍의 조짐이 없고, B는 마을 밖에서는 시원함이 실제라고 했으므로 틀리며, C는 들판이 되살아나는 듯하다는 묘사와 반대된다.

g.passage:
In each black little seed is a whole vine packed away.

After a time the old vine will fade away. It will fall and turn brown. It will do no more work of changing gases and minerals into living plant. It will not again have green leaves and bear bright flowers.

But there will be more morning-glories, for the vine has stored some of its life in the seeds, and they will not fade and cease to work. All that is left of the life of the vine is in the seeds. All the morning-glories that will grow and delight us with their bright flowers next summer lie packed away in the dark seeds.

Dear little seeds, live on through the cold winter; without you we never again could see our bright morning-glories!

options: the continuation of the vine's life after the old vine fades away.
the harsh winter that destroys every flower in the garden each year.
the work of changing gases and minerals into green leaves and flowers.

'All that is left of the life of the vine is in the seeds'라는 문장도 씨앗이 생명의 이어짐을 상징함을 보여 주므로 A가 정답이다. B는 씨앗이 겨울을 견디는 존재이지 겨울 자체가 아니라서 틀리다. C는 시드는 늙은 덩굴이 하던 일이고, D는 씨앗의 색만 보고 의미를 잘못 읽은 것이다.

g.passage: I rode up to the house and dismounted, hitched my horse to a post at the door, and proceeded to ring the bell. A tall, stately lady made her appearance, and invited me in with much apparent courtesy. She was dressed in deep mourning, which was very becoming to her pale, sad face. She seemed to be about thirty years of age, very prepossessing in appearance, and evidently belonged to one of the "F. F. V's." As soon as I was seated she inquired: "To what fortunate circumstance am I to attribute the pleasure of this unexpected call?" I told her in a few words the nature of my business. The intelligence seemed to cast a deep shadow over her pale features, which all her efforts could not control.

g.passage:
In a few minutes twenty-five hundred men were in simultaneous movement. Five companies of cavalry wheeled into column of companies, and advanced at a trot through the fields, seeking to gain the shelter of the forest. The six infantry regiments slid up alongside of each other, and pushed on in six parallel columns of march, two on the right of the road and four on the left. The artillery, which alone left the highway, followed at a distance of two or three hundred yards. The remaining cavalry made a wide detour to the right as if to flank the enemy’s left.

It was a mile and a quarter--it was a march of fully twenty minutes--to the edge of the woodland, the proposed cover of the column.

options: that the regiments moved into position smoothly and in close order.
that the soldiers lost their footing on the wet and muddy road.
that the regiments retreated quietly to avoid the enemy's notice.
that the soldiers mixed together until the columns could not be told apart.
g.explanation: 이 구절 앞에서는 'twenty-five hundred men were in simultaneous movement'라고 하여 대규모 부대가 함께 움직이는 장면을 보여 준다. 뒤이어 연대들이 'six parallel columns of march'로 나아갔다고 하므로, 'slid up'은 미끄러지듯 매끄럽게 나란히 정렬한 움직임을 뜻한다. 따라서 A가 정답이다. B는 문자 그대로 미끄러졌다고 읽은 오해이고, C는 부대가 전진하므로 틀리며, D는 평행한 대열이 유지되었다는 내용과 반대된다.

excerpt.text:
In a few minutes twenty-five hundred men were in simultaneous movement. Five companies of cavalry wheeled into column of companies, and advanced at a trot through the fields, seeking to gain the shelter of the forest. The six infantry regiments slid up alongside of each other, and pushed on in six parallel columns of march, two on the right of the road and four on the left. The artillery, which alone left the highway, followed at a distance of two or three hundred yards. The remaining cavalry made a wide detour to the right as if to flank the enemy’s left.

It was a mile and a quarter--it was a march of fully twenty minutes--to the edge of the woodland, the proposed cover of the column.

g.passage: A look of wild amazement swept over her face. It had not disappeared with her touch. It smiled upon her yet. No venomous thing had sprung from those parted and smiling lips. It was herself gazing upon herself. She was there—and it was there—oh! how that poor brain worked and toiled to solve the question of its double self. Was she, the creature of pain, with her temples full of fire, which had no power to melt the snow from her hair, an evil growth from the loveliness before her, and that perfect still? After wandering so many years, with age upon her limbs, and a curse at her heart, had she come back upon her own young self to be met with smiles and pleasant looks, as if no wickedness had ever crept between them?
g.question: As used in the text, the phrase “temples full of fire” most nearly suggests
options: that the woman is filled with fierce anger at her own reflection.
that the woman is suffering from a burning, feverish pain in her head.
that the woman has recently escaped from a house that caught fire.
that the woman's hair has been darkened and scorched by the heat.
g.explanation: 지문은 그녀를 'the creature of pain'이라고 부르며 이 구절을 쓰고, 그 불이 'had no power to melt the snow from her hair'라고 덧붙인다. 또 'that poor brain worked and toiled'라는 표현이 머리의 고통과 혼란을 강조하므로, 관자놀이 속 불은 열에 들뜬 듯한 머리의 고통을 뜻한다. 따라서 B가 정답이다. A는 그녀가 분노보다 놀라움과 혼란을 느끼므로 틀리고, C와 D는 비유를 실제 화재로 오해한 것이다.

g.passage:
There the old armorial stones dwellers seldom read;
There the ivy clambers like the rankest weed;
There the Cambridge lawyers sometimes scale the wall
To the grave of Helen, loveliest of all.

Even here the fairest of the little band
Strangers call the fairest girls in Maryland,
Like the peach her color ere its dyes are fast,
And her form as slender as the virgin mast.

Like a vessel gliding with a net in tow,
Up the street of evenings Helen seemed to flow,
Leaving light behind her and a nameless spell
Murmured in the young men, like an ocean shell.
g.question: As used in the text, the phrase “like an ocean shell” most nearly suggests
options: that Helen spoke to the young men in a loud and commanding voice.
that the young men collected shells as gifts to win Helen's favor.
that Helen's charm lingered in the young men like a faint echo.
that the young men feared Helen as sailors fear a stormy ocean.
g.explanation: 시는 Helen이 거리를 흐르듯 지나가며 'Leaving light behind her and a nameless spell'을 남긴다고 묘사한다. 그 매력이 젊은이들 속에서 소라 껍데기처럼 'Murmured'한다는 것은 그녀가 떠난 뒤에도 은은한 울림처럼 남는다는 뜻이므로 C가 정답이다. A는 'murmured'라는 낮은 소리와 맞지 않고, B는 비유를 실제 조개 수집으로 오해했다. D는 시 전체가 그녀의 아름다움을 찬미하므로 두려움과 거리가 멀다.

g.passage:
Sometimes it charms us; sometimes it repels. But we can no more be oblivious to it than we can to the temperature of the air. Its possessor has but to enter the room, and insensibly we are conscious of a presence. It is as if we had suddenly been placed in the field of a magnetic force.

On the other hand there are people who produce no effect upon us whatever. They come and go with a like indifference. They are as unimportant psychically as if they were any other portion of the furniture. They never stir us. We might live with them for fifty years and be hardly able to tell, for any influence upon ourselves, whether they existed or not.
g.question: As used in the text, the phrase “placed in the field of a magnetic force” most nearly suggests
options: that such a person exerts a strong, invisible pull on everyone nearby.
that such a person makes others feel physically uncomfortable and hot.
that such a person works in a laboratory studying electricity and magnets.
that such a person forces others to agree with whatever is said aloud.
g.explanation: 필자는 그런 사람이 방에 들어오기만 해도 'insensibly we are conscious of a presence'라고 말한다. 반대로 영향력 없는 사람들은 'They never stir us'라고 대비되므로, 자기장 비유는 눈에 보이지 않지만 강하게 끌어당기는 존재감을 뜻한다. 따라서 A가 정답이다. B는 기온 비유를 신체적 불편으로 잘못 읽었고, C는 비유를 문자 그대로 받아들였으며, D는 끌림이 'charms us'일 수도 'repels'일 수도 있다는 내용과 맞지 않는다.

g.passage: All at once--strange as it may seem, it is true,--the vessel stopped, in the mid sea, as fast as if it was fixed on the ground. The men, astonished, pulled at their oars, and spread more sail, trying to make progress by the aid of both, but all in vain. Ivy twined round the oars and hindered their motion, and clung to the sails, with heavy clusters of berries. A vine, laden with grapes, ran up the mast, and along the sides of the vessel. The sound of flutes was heard and the odor of fragrant wine spread all around.
g.question: As used in the text, the phrase “as fast as if it was fixed on the ground” most nearly suggests
options: that the vessel was moving at a great speed across the open sea.
that the vessel stopped completely, as though held by solid land.
that the vessel had run aground on a hidden sandbar near the coast.
that the vessel slowed gradually as the wind died down around it.
g.explanation: 지문은 배가 'in the mid sea'에서 갑자기 멈췄다고 하므로 실제 육지에 걸린 것이 아니다. 선원들이 노를 젓고 돛을 더 펼쳐도 'all in vain'이었다는 점에서, 이 비유는 배가 땅에 고정된 듯 꼼짝 않고 멈춘 상태를 뜻한다. 따라서 B가 정답이다. A는 'fast'를 속도로 오해한 것이고, C는 바다 한가운데라는 설정과 맞지 않으며, D는 갑작스러운 정지를 점진적 감속으로 바꾸어 틀리다.
